content: Misoprostol, when administered orally in low doses (≤ 50 µg), is a widely used method for inducing labor. Higher doses of misoprostol are associated with an unacceptably high risk of uterine hyperstimulation, which is why this review focuses on low-dose regimens. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of low-dose oral misoprostol for labor induction in women with a viable fetus during the third trimester of pregnancy. The review included 61 randomized trials involving 20,026 women. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low certainty, with limitations due to imprecision, inconsistency, and methodological issues in the included studies. Oral Misoprostol vs. Placebo or No Treatment In four trials involving 594 women, oral misoprostol may have little to no effect on the rate of cesarean sections (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.11; moderate-certainty evidence). However, its impact on uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes remains uncertain (RR 5.15, 95% CI 0.25 to 105.31; very low-certainty evidence). Vaginal births within 24 hours were not reported in these trials. All participants had pre-labor ruptured membranes, and oxytocin was allowed to be initiated after 12 to 24 hours. Oral Misoprostol vs. Vaginal Dinoprostone Thirteen trials involving 9,676 women showed that oral misoprostol likely reduces the rate of cesarean sections compared to vaginal dinoprostone (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.90; moderate-certainty evidence). Subgroup analysis suggested that lower doses of oral misoprostol (10 µg to 25 µg) were more effective in reducing cesarean sections (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87) compared to higher doses (50 µg) (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.34). Oral misoprostol may slightly reduce the likelihood of vaginal births within 24 hours (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.00; low-certainty evidence) and may also lower the risk of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.59; low-certainty evidence). Oral Misoprostol vs. Vaginal Misoprostol In 33 trials involving 6,110 women, oral misoprostol may result in fewer vaginal births within 24 hours (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.95; low-certainty evidence) and less uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.92; low-certainty evidence). Subgroup analysis indicated that lower doses of oral misoprostol (10 µg to 25 µg) were associated with significantly lower rates of hyperstimulation (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.57) compared to higher doses (50 µg) (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11). Oral misoprostol likely does not increase the overall rate of cesarean sections (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.16; low-certainty evidence) but may reduce cesarean sections performed due to fetal distress (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99). Oral Misoprostol vs. Intravenous Oxytocin Six trials involving 737 women (200 with ruptured membranes) showed that oral misoprostol may have little to no effect on the likelihood of vaginal births within 24 hours (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.33; low-certainty evidence). However, it likely reduces the rate of cesarean sections (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.90; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of oral misoprostol on uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes is uncertain (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.26; very low-certainty evidence). Oral Misoprostol vs. Mechanical Methods Six trials involving 2,993 women compared oral misoprostol to the use of a transcervical Foley catheter. Oral misoprostol may increase the likelihood of vaginal birth within 24 hours (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.79; low-certainty evidence) and likely reduces the rate of cesarean sections (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.95; moderate-certainty evidence). There may be little to no difference in the risk of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.21; low-certainty evidence). Different Oral Misoprostol Regimens One trial involving 64 women compared oneto two-hourly dosing with fourto six-hourly dosing, but the evidence was very uncertain due to the small sample size. Two trials involving 296 women compared a 20 µg hourly titrated regimen to a 25 µg two-hourly static regimen. The difference in vaginal births within 24 hours was minimal (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.16; low-certainty evidence), and the evidence for other outcomes was of very low certainty. Conclusions Low-dose oral misoprostol is likely associated with fewer cesarean sections and lower rates of uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes compared to vaginal dinoprostone. However, it may result in fewer vaginal births within 24 hours, indicating a longer time to delivery. Compared to the transcervical Foley catheter, oral misoprostol is associated with fewer cesarean sections but similar rates of uterine hyperstimulation. When compared to vaginal misoprostol, oral administration likely results in similar overall rates of vaginal birth but with fewer cases of hyperstimulation and fewer cesarean sections due to fetal distress. The findings suggest that low-dose oral misoprostol offers several advantages over other methods for labor induction. A starting dose of 25 µg may provide an optimal balance between efficacy and safety. However, further research is needed to determine the most effective and safe dosing regimen for oral misoprostol.
